title: SDS 940 — Complete Overview
body:
The SDS 940 is a early computer record of the 1966 era, originating with Scientific Data Systems.

24-bit timesharing machine; the Tymshare network and early ARPANET IMPs' cousin. GENIE project at Berkeley proved timesharing commercially; sold to Xerox (1969). Influenced the SDS Sigma series.

Key specifications: Word: 24-bit; Memory: 16K–64K words; Use: Timesharing services.

Notable examples include SDS 940 (1966), SDS Sigma 7 (1966). This record is the front door of the database: start here, then follow the teaching ladder from the simple definition (record 2) through the engineering deep-dives (records 4–6) to the advanced restoration and collecting guides.

title: What Is SDS 940? — Definition
body:
Early computers are the electronic machines of roughly 1940–1965: room-sized systems built from vacuum tubes, then transistors, that computed with punched cards, paper tape, magnetic drums, and core memory. They include wartime codebreakers and calculators (Colossus, ENIAC), the first stored-program machines (EDSAC, Manchester Baby, EDVAC), and the first commercial systems (UNIVAC I, IBM 650/701/1401) that moved computing out of the laboratory and into business and government.

In the context of this database, the SDS 940 is presented as one early computer record among the early computers family. 24-bit timesharing machine; the Tymshare network and early ARPANET IMPs' cousin.

title: Origins and History of SDS 940
body:
The SDS 940 belongs to the 1966 era and traces to Scientific Data Systems.

War made the computer: Colossus (1943) broke Lorenz ciphers with 2,400 tubes; ENIAC (1945) computed artillery tables with 17,468 tubes and was programmed by plugging cables. The stored-program idea — von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report, building on Turing — let instructions live in memory like data. Manchester's Baby (1948) ran the first stored program; EDSAC (1949) was the first practical one. UNIVAC I (1951) predicted the Eisenhower election on TV and sold 46 systems; IBM's 650 (1954) rented by the thousand and taught industry data processing. Transistors arrived with the IBM 7090 (1959) and DEC PDP-1 (1960); integrated circuits with System/360 (1964), which unified a whole product line on one architecture — the decision that made IBM dominant. By the late 1960s, minicomputers (PDP-8, Nova) put computers in labs, and timesharing put terminals on desks.

Within that longer story, SDS 940: GENIE project at Berkeley proved timesharing commercially; sold to Xerox (1969). Influenced the SDS Sigma series.

title: How SDS 940 Works
body:
Early machines computed in binary (or decimal, like ENIAC and the IBM 650) with vacuum-tube flip-flops forming registers and adders. Programs were stored as patterns in memory — mercury delay lines (UNIVAC, EDSAC), Williams tubes (Manchester, IAS), or magnetic drums — and a control unit fetched, decoded, and executed instructions one by one: the fetch-decode-execute cycle still used today. Input came from punched cards or paper tape; output went to printers, punched cards, or magnetic tape (UNIVAC's UNISERVO). Clock speeds were kilohertz; an addition took microseconds to milliseconds. Programmers wrote machine code, then assembly, then early compilers (FORTRAN, 1957) and business languages (COBOL, 1959).

Applied to the SDS 940 (1966, Scientific Data Systems): Influenced the SDS Sigma series.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of SDS 940 — Components
body:
Every SDS 940 is an assembly of the early computers family's standard parts:

• Vacuum-tube flip-flop — Bistable circuit storing one bit; thousands per machine.
• Mercury delay line — Acoustic memory: bits as sound pulses circulating in mercury tubes.
• Williams tube — CRT-based memory storing bits as charged spots on phosphor.
• Magnetic drum — Rotating cylinder with read/write heads; early main working memory.
• Core memory — Woven ferrite rings holding bits magnetically; dominant 1955–1975.
• Card reader/punch — Hollerith 80-column punched cards in and out.
• Paper tape reader — 5–8 channel punched tape for programs and data.
• Line printer — Chain or drum printer hammering full lines at hundreds of lines per minute.
• Magnetic tape drive — UNISERVO and IBM 729 reels; the first mass storage.
• Console — Switches, lights, and meters — the operator's window into the machine.

When examining a surviving SDS 940, identify these parts in order: Vacuum-tube flip-flop, Mercury delay line, Williams tube, Magnetic drum, Core memory, Card reader/punch.

title: Early Computers — Historical Timeline
body:
Milestones in the history of early computers:

• 1943 — Colossus Mark 1 operational at Bletchley Park.
• 1945 — ENIAC completed; von Neumann's EDVAC report circulates.
• 1948 — Manchester Baby runs the first stored program (June 21).
• 1949 — EDSAC operational; first practical stored-program computer.
• 1951 — UNIVAC I delivered to the Census Bureau; predicts 1952 election.
• 1954 — IBM 650 announced — the Model T of computers, ~2,000 installed.
• 1957 — FORTRAN released; first successful high-level language.
• 1959 — IBM 7090: transistorized scientific workhorse; COBOL specified.
• 1960 — DEC PDP-1 ships; Spacewar! follows at MIT.
• 1964 — System/360 announced — one architecture, a whole product line.

The SDS 940 (1966) sits on this timeline at: 24-bit timesharing machine; the Tymshare network and early ARPANET IMPs' cousin..

title: Key Figures Behind Early Computers
body:
The people who made early computers possible:

• John von Neumann (1903–1957) — EDVAC report author; stored-program architecture bears his name.
• J. Presper Eckert & John Mauchly — ENIAC and UNIVAC builders; founded the commercial computer industry.
• Alan Turing (1912–1954) — 1936 universal machine theory; wartime Bombe work at Bletchley Park.
• Tommy Flowers (1905–1998) — Built Colossus at Dollis Hill; electronic switching for codebreaking.
• Maurice Wilkes (1913–2010) — Built EDSAC; wrote the first practical stored-program computer into history.
• Grace Hopper (1906–1992) — A-0 compiler, FLOW-MATIC, COBOL; 'bug' popularizer and evangelist.
• Gene Amdahl (1922–2015) — Chief architect of System/360; later Amdahl's law.
• Seymour Cray (1925–1996) — CDC 1604/6600 designer; the father of supercomputing.

SDS 940 originates with Scientific Data Systems, standing on the work of the figures above.

title: Early Computers Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of early computers:

• stored program — Instructions held in memory as data; the defining idea of the modern computer.
• word — The natural data unit of a machine (e.g., 36-bit on IBM 709, 12-bit on PDP-8).
• accumulator — Register holding arithmetic results; ENIAC had 20 of them.
• bootstrap — Tiny hardwired loader that pulls in the real program — 'pulling up by bootstraps'.
• batch processing — Jobs queued on cards/tape and run in batches; no interaction.
• timesharing — Many terminals sharing one machine interactively (1960s).
• core dump — Printout of memory contents for debugging — from core memory.
• patch — Literally a patch cord rerouting on plugboards; the word stuck.
• bug — Grace Hopper's 1947 moth in the Harvard Mark II relay — the logbook page is famous.
• uptime — Machines like ENIAC ran ~50% uptime; tubes failed constantly.
• MTBF — Mean time between failures; tube machines measured it in hours.
• drum memory — Rotating-drum storage; programmers optimized code placement ('drum latency coding').

title: SDS 940 in Culture
body:
Early computers are cathedral-sized oracles: flashing consoles, spinning reels, operators in white shirts tending machines like steam engines. They promised 'electronic brains' in newsreels and threatened them in science fiction. ENIAC's 'giant brain' headlines, UNIVAC's election-night prediction, the SAGE radar network's Cold War watchfulness — computing entered public imagination as both servant and sentinel. The plugboard programmers of ENIAC — six women mathematicians — are now rightly famous as the first programmers.

The SDS 940 carries that cultural charge directly: Influenced the SDS Sigma series.

title: Collecting and Preserving SDS 940
body:
Whole early mainframes are museum-scale; collectors focus on modules, core planes, front panels, plugboard cables, card decks, manuals, and console furniture. Provenance matters enormously. Core memory planes are beautiful and display well. Paper documentation — maintenance manuals, program listings — is often rarer than hardware.

For the SDS 940 specifically: 24-bit timesharing machine; the Tymshare network and early ARPANET IMPs' cousin.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working SDS 940 with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: SDS 940 Restoration Guide
body:
Tube machines need wholesale capacitor replacement and careful variac bring-up; unobtainium tubes must be sourced before powering. Core and drum systems are mechanically delicate — bearings, heads, and alignment. Bit-rot in documentation is the real killer: scan everything. Restorations at Bletchley (Colossus) and CHM set the gold standard: document every wire before disturbing it.

Restoration order for a SDS 940: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical early computer record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: SDS 940 — Stored-program mini-machine emulator (Runnable Python)
body:
A tiny fetch-decode-execute emulator in the spirit of the Manchester Baby/EDSAC: 16 words of memory, 4 instructions, runs a real program that adds two numbers.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the SDS 940 so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Baby/EDSAC-spirit 16-word stored-program emulator (public-domain concept)
# Instructions: 0=HALT, 1=LOAD addr, 2=ADD addr, 3=STORE addr. Addresses 0-15.

def run(mem):
    mem = mem[:] + [0] * (16 - len(mem))
    acc, pc, steps = 0, 0, 0
    trace = []
    while steps < 200:
        instr = mem[pc] // 16 % 16   # high nibble = opcode (toy encoding)
        addr = mem[pc] % 16          # low nibble = address
        op = mem[pc]
        opcode, addr = op // 16, op % 16
        trace.append(f"pc={pc:02d} op={opcode} addr={addr:02d} acc={acc}")
        pc += 1
        if opcode == 0:
            break
        elif opcode == 1:
            acc = mem[addr]
        elif opcode == 2:
            acc += mem[addr]
        elif opcode == 3:
            mem[addr] = acc
        steps += 1
    return acc, mem, trace

# Program: LOAD 14, ADD 15, STORE 13, HALT ; data: 14->40, 15->2
prog = [0]*16
prog[0] = 1*16 + 14   # LOAD 14
prog[1] = 2*16 + 15   # ADD 15
prog[2] = 3*16 + 13   # STORE 13
prog[3] = 0*16 + 0    # HALT
prog[14], prog[15] = 40, 2
acc, mem, trace = run(prog)
print("\n".join(trace))
print(f"RESULT: 40 + 2 = {mem[13]} (accumulator={acc})")
